topics.title: Password Spraying
topics.content: Password spraying is the technique of trying a single password against many user accounts simultaneously, minimizing the risk of account lockouts compared to brute-force attacks. NXC supports spraying via 'nxc smb <dc_ip> -u users.txt -p Password123'. By default, NXC stops after the first successful authentication. The --continue-on-success flag is critical — it makes NXC continue testing all users even after finding valid credentials. Without this flag, you will miss other valid accounts. The --no-bruteforce flag changes the behavior to pair each username with its corresponding password line-by-line (user1:pass1, user2:pass2) rather than trying all combinations. CRITICAL: Always retrieve the password policy (--pass-pol) before spraying. Safe spraying formula: try at most (lockout_threshold - 2) passwords per reset_counter period. For example, if lockout threshold is 5 and reset counter is 30 minutes, try 3 passwords maximum, then wait 35+ minutes before the next round. Common effective passwords: Season+Year (Summer2024!), CompanyName+123, Month+Year, Password+Number, Welcome+Number. Spray against the DC (not individual hosts) since all domain auth goes through the DC anyway — this reduces event volume. Reduce threads with -t 1 for stealth. The --jitter flag adds a random delay between attempts.

topics.title: Credential Validation Across Multiple Hosts
topics.content: Once valid credentials are obtained (through spraying, cracking, phishing, or any other method), the next step is checking where those credentials grant access across the network. Running 'nxc smb <subnet> -u user -p pass' authenticates to every host and shows [+] for success and (Pwn3d!) for admin access. This is one of the most powerful NXC capabilities — instantly mapping where a single set of credentials can be used for lateral movement. For local admin password reuse testing, use --local-auth to check if a local admin password is shared across multiple workstations. Common findings include: service accounts with local admin on multiple servers, the same local admin password across all workstations (pre-LAPS environments), domain admin credentials with Pwn3d! on every host. Check multiple protocols (SMB, WinRM, RDP, MSSQL) to find all access paths. The nxcdb database automatically stores all successful authentications, making it easy to query which credentials work where.

topics.title: Pass-the-Hash (PTH)
topics.content: Pass-the-Hash (PTH) allows authentication using NTLM hashes without knowing the plaintext password. This is one of the most critical lateral movement techniques because NTLM hashes are available from SAM dumps, LSASS dumps, and NTDS dumps. NXC accepts hashes via -H in two formats: the full LM:NT format ('aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99') or just the NT hash ('5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99'). The LM hash portion is almost always 'aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee' (empty LM hash) on modern systems since LM hashing is disabled by default. PTH works because NTLM authentication uses the NT hash directly — the DC/host never sees the plaintext password. PTH requirements: the target must accept NTLM authentication (not Kerberos-only), and for administrative operations the account must be local admin on the target. For the built-in Administrator (RID 500), PTH always works for admin operations even with UAC remote restrictions. For other local admin accounts, the registry key LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy must be set to 1. PTH works regardless of SMB signing — signing prevents relay attacks, not direct hash authentication. Hashes can be sprayed across subnets just like passwords: 'nxc smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u administrator -H hash --local-auth'.

topics.title: Pass-the-Ticket (PTT) with Kerberos
topics.content: Pass-the-Ticket (PTT) uses Kerberos tickets (.ccache files) for authentication instead of passwords or NTLM hashes. This technique is stealthier than PTH because it uses legitimate Kerberos authentication, avoiding NTLM-specific detections (Event ID 4776 on the DC). To use PTT with NXC: 1) Set the KRB5CCNAME environment variable to point to the .ccache ticket file, 2) Use -k to enable Kerberos authentication and --use-kcache to use the cached ticket. CRITICAL: targets must be specified by hostname (not IP) because Kerberos requires hostname resolution. The .ccache file can contain a TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) or a service-specific TGS. TGTs can be obtained through: impacket's getTGT.py, Rubeus on Windows, or extracted from memory. Golden tickets (forged TGTs using the krbtgt hash) and silver tickets (forged TGS for specific services) can also be used with PTT. Requirements: /etc/krb5.conf must be configured or DNS must resolve the domain, the ticket must be valid and not expired, and clock skew must be less than 5 minutes between the attacker and the DC. Kerberos PTT generates Event IDs 4768 (TGT request) and 4769 (TGS request) instead of NTLM events.

topics.title: Kerberoasting via NXC
topics.content: Kerberoasting extracts Kerberos service ticket hashes (TGS) for accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs), which can then be cracked offline to reveal service account passwords. Any domain user can request service tickets — no special privileges are needed. NXC performs Kerberoasting via the LDAP module: 'nxc ldap <dc> -u user -p pass --kerberoasting output.txt'. The output lists discovered SPNs (e.g., svc_sql - MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433) and writes hashcat/john-compatible hashes to the output file in the format $krb5tgs$23$*username$DOMAIN$SPN*$hash. Crack with hashcat mode 13100: 'hashcat -m 13100 output.txt rockyou.txt'. Service accounts are high-value targets because they often have: weak passwords (set once and never changed), elevated privileges (local admin on multiple servers), and SPNs that make them Kerberoastable. Common Kerberoastable SPNs include MSSQLSvc (SQL Server), HTTP (web services), cifs (file sharing), and custom SPNs. Defense: use long, random passwords (25+ characters) for service accounts, use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) where possible, and monitor for Event ID 4769 with RC4 encryption (0x17) as a Kerberoasting indicator.

RC4 encryption (0x17) in TGS requests is a strong detection indicator

best_practices: Any domain user can Kerberoast — it's often the first escalation step
Focus cracking efforts on service accounts that are likely admin somewhere
Use rules and large wordlists — service account passwords may be complex but not necessarily long

topics.title: AS-REP Roasting via NXC
topics.content: AS-REP Roasting targets accounts that have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH user account control flag). When pre-authentication is disabled, anyone can request an AS-REP (Authentication Service Reply) for that account without providing a password, and the response contains an encrypted portion that can be cracked offline. NXC performs AS-REP roasting via the LDAP module: 'nxc ldap <dc> -u user -p pass --asreproast output.txt'. The output identifies accounts with UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set and writes hashes in the format $krb5asrep$23$username@DOMAIN:hash. Crack with hashcat mode 18200: 'hashcat -m 18200 output.txt rockyou.txt'. Unlike Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting can be performed without valid domain credentials — you only need a list of usernames. Use 'nxc ldap <dc> -u users.txt -p '' --asreproast output.txt' to check a username list without passwords. Accounts with pre-auth disabled are relatively rare in well-managed environments but are common in legacy configurations and environments with older applications that don't support pre-authentication. AS-REP hashes use encryption type 23 (RC4) by default and are faster to crack than Kerberoast hashes.

topics.title: Secretsdump: SAM, LSA, and NTDS
topics.content: NXC can extract credentials from three sources: the SAM database, LSA secrets, and the NTDS.dit Active Directory database. SAM dump (--sam) extracts local user account hashes from the Security Accounts Manager registry hive. Output format: username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash:::. Requires local admin on the target. Use these hashes for PTH against other hosts to test local admin password reuse. LSA secrets dump (--lsa) extracts cached domain credentials (DCC2 format), service account passwords, machine account hashes, and DPAPI keys. DCC2 hashes are much slower to crack (hashcat mode 2100). NTDS dump (--ntds) performs a DCSync attack, extracting the entire Active Directory database including all user hashes. This uses the MS-DRSR (Directory Replication Service Remote) protocol to impersonate a domain controller requesting replication data. Requirements: Domain Admin, Enterprise Admin, or specific 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' permissions. Output format: DOMAIN\username:RID:LM:NT:::. Optional flags: --ntds-pwdLastSet adds the password last set date to each entry, --ntds-history dumps previous password hashes for password reuse analysis. DCSync is detectable via Event ID 4662 with specific replication GUIDs from a non-DC source IP. DCSync does not require code execution on the DC — it works purely over the network via RPC.

topics.title: Command Execution Methods
topics.content: NXC supports four methods for executing commands on remote hosts, each with different OPSEC characteristics. wmiexec (default) uses WMI/DCOM — no service created, output via temp file on ADMIN$, requires DCOM (port 135 + high ports), generates WMI-Activity events. smbexec creates a temporary Windows service — very noisy (Event ID 7045 for service creation), only requires SMB (port 445), leaves clear artifacts in System event log. atexec uses the Task Scheduler — creates/deletes a scheduled task (Event IDs 4698/4699), moderate detection risk, blends with legitimate scheduled tasks. mmcexec uses MMC DCOM objects — no service created, requires DCOM, less commonly monitored than WMI. Specify the method with --exec-method: 'nxc smb target -u admin -p pass -x whoami --exec-method atexec'. Use -x for cmd.exe commands and -X for PowerShell commands. All methods require local admin access (Pwn3d!). Commands can be executed across entire subnets: 'nxc smb 192.168.1.0/24 -u admin -p pass -x hostname'. For OPSEC: prefer wmiexec (no service), avoid smbexec (service creation is the strongest detection signal). For compatibility: use smbexec when DCOM is blocked, use atexec as a middle ground.

topics.title: File Transfer Operations
topics.content: NXC supports file upload and download via SMB shares. The --put-file flag uploads a local file to the target: 'nxc smb target -u admin -p pass --put-file /local/path/file.exe C:\remote\path\file.exe'. The --get-file flag downloads a file from the target: 'nxc smb target -u admin -p pass --get-file C:\remote\path\file.txt /local/path/file.txt'. Both operations require appropriate permissions — typically local admin for writing to system directories. Common use cases: uploading tools (SharpHound, Rubeus, ProcDump) for execution, downloading sensitive files (web.config, KeePass databases, registry hives), and exfiltrating data. File transfers use SMB (CIFS) protocol and generate Event ID 5145 for share access. Always clean up uploaded files after use to reduce artifacts. For operational security, avoid uploading well-known offensive tools to disk — they may be caught by AV/EDR file scanning. Instead, prefer in-memory execution when possible or use renamed/obfuscated binaries.
